prompt: Do comparison pages help a product show up in AI answers?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Yes—good comparison pages can help your product appear in AI answers, especially when buyers ask “X vs. Y,” “alternatives to X,” or “which tool fits my needs?”** Treat them as useful buying guidance, with AI visibility as an additional benefit.

The rationale: AI search retrieves relevant web pages to support its answers. A comparison page directly addresses those buying questions and supplies facts the answer can use. That’s a reasonable inference from [Google’s explanation of how AI search retrieves content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), **not evidence that comparison pages receive a special ranking boost.**

For a product marketing team, I’d recommend:

- **Start with three to five real competitive decisions.** Use competitors and questions that repeatedly appear in sales calls, lost deals, and customer interviews.
- **Explain who each product suits.** Include situations where the competitor is the better choice. Avoid tables where your product wins every row.
- **Provide verifiable details.** Compare pricing assumptions, plan restrictions, integrations, implementation effort, and specific workflows. Link to evidence and show when facts were checked.
- **Give readers a clear answer.** Open with the main differences, then support them with a comparison table and concrete examples. These help buyers; they aren’t guaranteed AI citation tricks.
- **Keep the pages accessible and maintained.** Google says foundational SEO and unique, helpful content remain central to AI search visibility; special AI markup isn’t required. [Google guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)

**Measure three separate outcomes: product mentions, page citations, and qualified conversions.** An AI answer can cite your page without recommending your product.

Start with **Bing Webmaster Tools’ AI Performance report**, because it shows cited pages and the queries associated with citations across supported Microsoft and partner experiences. Supplement that with repeated checks of a fixed set of buyer questions across the AI services your audience uses. [Bing’s reporting documentation](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/ai-performance-9f8e7d6c)

I’d pilot a few strong pages before producing a large comparison library. Judge success by accurate inclusion in relevant buying conversations and pipeline impact—not citation counts alone.

prompt: How should we prioritize fixes to improve how AI assistants describe our product?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Rank each problem by **business impact × how often it appears × how easy it is to fix at the source.** In practice, fix factual errors on high-intent prompts first, then the sources AI tools pull from, and work on general visibility last.

## Step 0: Set a baseline (1–2 weeks)
You can't rank fixes until you know what the assistants actually say.
- Write 50–150 prompts that match how buyers really ask: category ("best X for Y"), comparison ("you vs. competitor"), problem-led, pricing, and integration questions.
- Run them on ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, Perplexity, Gemini, Claude and Copilot, and run them repeatedly. Answers shift a lot. A SISTRIX dataset reported by Search Engine Journal showed citation churn jumping to about 47% during one model update, against a normal 1–2% a day. That data came from German-language ChatGPT, so treat it as a rough signal, but one spot check tells you very little.
- **Tools:** **Peec AI** (about $80–90/mo) is a good default for tracking across several assistants. **Profound** fits if you're enterprise and need broad platform coverage and reporting. **Scrunch** (from about $250/mo) breaks visibility down by persona and intent. **Otterly.AI** (about $29/mo) is enough for a cheap pilot. If you already pay for Ahrefs, check **Ahrefs Brand Radar** first. Pricing in the roundups I found doesn't agree, so check vendor sites.

## Step 1: Sort what you find into three buckets
Each one needs a different kind of fix:
1. **Misinformation:** wrong pricing, features you dropped, the wrong category, confusion with another company.
2. **Unfavorable framing:** assistants repeat a competitor's positioning or an outdated weakness.
3. **Invisibility:** you don't come up on category prompts at all.

## Step 2: Priority order
| Priority | What to fix | Why first |
|---|---|---|
| **P0** | Factual errors on bottom-of-funnel prompts (pricing, core capabilities, security/compliance, integrations) | They lose deals directly and are usually the cheapest to fix |
| **P1** | The source documents behind those errors | Most errors trace back to a specific page: an old pricing page, a stale G2/Capterra/Crunchbase listing, an outdated partner or reseller page, an old press release. Fix the source, not just the symptom |
| **P2** | Consistency of basic facts everywhere | Your description, category, URL and key facts should match across your site, directories, review sites, Wikipedia/Wikidata if you qualify, LinkedIn and app marketplaces |
| **P3** | Competitive framing on comparison prompts | Publish honest, specific comparison pages and get third parties to back up your differentiators |
| **P4** | Visibility on broad category prompts | Earned media, analyst coverage, reviews, community mentions. Slowest to move and hardest to measure |

## Step 3: Specific moves
- **Look at citations before you write anything.** For each bad answer, check which URLs the assistant cites (Perplexity, AI Overviews and ChatGPT search all show them). Your fix list is mostly those URLs.
- **Prioritize third-party sources.** Practitioner write-ups citing 2025 research say AI search leans heavily on earned and third-party sources over brand-owned pages. A few strong placements in outlets the models already cite are worth more than many minor ones. Point PR and analyst relations at those outlets.
- **Make your own site easy to quote.** Keep pricing, feature, integration and FAQ pages current and in plain text, with one clear claim per section. Don't hide facts in PDFs or JavaScript, and don't block AI crawlers you want to be cited by in robots.txt.
- **Assign owners.** Web for owned pages, PR/AR for earned media, partner marketing for reseller and marketplace listings, customer marketing for reviews.

## Step 4: Measure
Re-run the same prompt set weekly or biweekly. Track accuracy rate (correct facts ÷ answers that mention you), share of voice on category prompts, and how often your preferred sources get cited. Expect weeks to months before fixes show up, and expect noise whenever a model updates.

**Caveat:** Almost everything published on this comes from vendors or agencies. I found no independent evidence on how reliably, or how fast, fixing sources changes AI answers. Run it as a test: fix a batch, measure, then put more money into what actually moved.

If you send me 3–5 examples of what assistants are getting wrong, I can help you sort them into the buckets and trace the likely sources.

**Sources:**
- [Gracker: Tools to check if ChatGPT mentions your brand](https://gracker.ai/blog/chatgpt-brand-mention-tools)
- [DesignRush: Tools for tracking LLM brand visibility](https://designrush.com/agency/ai-companies/trends/tools-for-tracking-llm-brand-visibility)

- [Marketful: AI visibility tools](https://marketful.com/ai-visibility-tools)

prompt: How long does it take for new content to change what ChatGPT and Perplexity say about us?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Short answer:** When ChatGPT or Perplexity searches the web for an answer, new content can show up within days to a few weeks. What the models "know" without searching only changes when a new model is trained and released, which takes months to more than a year. You can't speed that up. No independent benchmark exists for either timeline. The numbers below come from vendor and agency studies, so use them for rough planning only.

## The two paths

**1. Live search answers (where you can make a difference)**
- **Crawling:** In one small vendor test, OpenAI's search crawler (OAI-SearchBot) reached new pages in about 2 hours and Perplexity's crawler (PerplexityBot) in about 6 hours. About 43% of the 300 new pages were crawled within 24 hours ([Presenc](https://presenc.ai/research/how-fast-ai-crawlers-index-new-pages)).
- **Showing up in answers:** Vendor guides estimate about **1–3 weeks for ChatGPT**, and **2–4 weeks for Perplexity** after technical fixes like unblocking its crawler and adding structured data. Google AI Overviews takes about 4–8 weeks because it follows normal Google indexing ([WebSNP](https://www.websnp.com/help/how-to-get-cited-by-chatgpt-perplexity-ai-overviews), [Upgrowth](https://upgrowth.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/how-to-get-cited-by-perplexity-ai-slides-1.pdf)).
- Getting crawled doesn't mean getting cited. A page competes with every other source on the topic, so if established pages already rank, being indexed quickly won't win the citation by itself.

**2. What the model says without searching (slow)**
- This changes only when a new model version ships, typically months to a year or more after your content goes live. Brand descriptions that are widely repeated and consistent across the web have the best chance of making it in.

## Things that speed it up or block it
- **Don't block the search crawlers.** Check that robots.txt and your CDN or bot protection (e.g. Cloudflare) allow OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot. One vendor tracker says blocking OAI-SearchBot removes you from ChatGPT search citations ([Trakkr](https://www.trakkr.ai/data/crawlers/oai-searchbot)).
- **Put key content in the page's HTML.** These crawlers generally don't run JavaScript, so text loaded by scripts may never be seen ([Dupple](https://www.dupple.com/learn/ai-search-visibility-chatgpt-perplexity)).
- **Get indexed by Bing and Google.** Search-based answers lean on these indexes, so submit your sitemaps and use IndexNow for Bing.
- **Keep pages fresh.** Seer found that three in four cited pages had been updated within the past year, and that updating existing pages helps as much as publishing new ones ([Seer Interactive](https://www.seerinteractive.com/insights/study-content-recencys-impact-on-ai-visibility-in-2026)). Ahrefs found ChatGPT tends to cite newer pages ([Ahrefs](https://ahrefs.com/blog/do-ai-assistants-prefer-to-cite-fresh-content)).
- **Build comparison and alternatives pages.** One vendor found PerplexityBot spends an outsized share of its crawling on /compare and /alternatives URLs ([Presenc](https://presenc.ai/research/ai-crawler-fetch-frequency-by-page-type)).
- **Get mentioned on other sites.** Third-party mentions on review sites, Reddit, and in the press often get cited more than your own site.

## How to measure it
- **Server logs:** Check when OAI-SearchBot and PerplexityBot first request each new URL. This is your most reliable data.
- **Prompt tracking:** Run a fixed set of prompts every week. AI answers change a lot from one run to the next (Ahrefs saw AI Overview content change 70% of the time for the same query), so a single check tells you little. Tools like Profound, Peec AI, Otterly.ai, and Semrush's AI toolkit track this over time.
- **Referral traffic:** Watch for visits from chatgpt.com and perplexity.ai in your analytics.

**Planning rule of thumb:** If the crawlers can get in, expect search-based answers to start reflecting new or updated content in about 2–4 weeks, and judge results at 6–8 weeks. Changing what the models say without searching is a long-term effort tied to new model releases.

Other sources: [Get-Ryze on recrawl frequency](https://www.get-ryze.ai/blog/how-often-do-chatgpt-and-perplexity-recrawl-and-how-to-force-a-refresh), [Techwyse on OpenAI crawler growth](https://www.techwyse.com/news/ai-search/openai-crawlers-tripled-gpt5-log-file-analysis), [Whitehat SEO engine comparison](https://whitehat-seo.co.uk/blog/ai-engines-comparison-citations)

prompt: ChatGPT keeps recommending our competitor instead of us. What can we actually do about it?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
You can't pay ChatGPT or ask it to change its answers. What you can change is the material it learns from and the web pages it pulls up when it searches. Paid ads are a separate route, and buying them won't change the answer itself.

## 1. Measure first (1–2 weeks)
Find out why it picks the competitor before you change anything.
- **Write 30–100 real buyer prompts**, such as "best X for Y," "[competitor] alternatives," and "[you] vs [competitor]." Run them in ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews.
- **Log three things for each answer:** who gets recommended, the reasons given, and **which sources are cited**. The citations are what you act on.
- **Tools:** HubSpot's free AEO Grader gives a quick snapshot. For ongoing tracking, Peec AI or Otterly.AI cost roughly $50–$300/month. If you need prompt-level share-of-voice and citation analysis at enterprise scale, Profound or Scrunch run about $1K–$4K+/month. Semrush AI Visibility makes sense if you already pay for Semrush. These prices come from vendor and agency comparisons, so check them yourself.

## 2. Fix what the cited sources say (biggest lever)
When ChatGPT searches the web, it leans on third-party pages, not your homepage. You'll usually find the competitor winning because of:
- **Listicles and "best X" roundups.** Pitch the authors, ask to be added, and offer updated information.
- **Review sites** like G2, Capterra and TrustRadius. Run a campaign to collect fresh reviews, and fill out your profiles and category tags completely.
- **Reddit, Quora, YouTube and forums.** Answer real threads as yourself and say you're from the company, not as fake customers. Get customers and partners talking about you.
- **Wikipedia, analyst reports and comparison pages.** Make sure you're present and the details are accurate.

## 3. Make your own site easy to quote
- **Write clear category statements.** "[Product] is a [category] for [audience] that [differentiator]." Use the same wording on every page and channel.
- **Publish honest comparison and alternatives pages**, such as "[You] vs [Competitor]" and "[Competitor] alternatives." Models quote these heavily.
- **Put pricing, specs, integrations and FAQs in plain HTML**, not behind JavaScript, PDFs or gated forms. Add schema markup.
- **Don't block AI crawlers.** Check robots.txt for OAI-SearchBot, GPTBot and the others.
- **Correct wrong or outdated claims** wherever they appear. If ChatGPT says you "lack feature Z," find out where that came from.

## 4. Consider ChatGPT ads (separate from the answer)
OpenAI started showing ads in February 2026. They're labeled "Sponsored," sit below the answer, and only appear for Free and Go users, not Plus, Pro or Business. Reports say a self-serve Ads Manager with CPC bidding has been open to US businesses since May 2026. OpenAI says ads don't influence the answer, so treat them as a way to show up next to the competitor's mention, not to replace it. Check OpenAI's own documentation for current markets and formats, because reports differ.

## 5. Set realistic timing
- Answers that rely on web search can change within weeks once the cited pages change.
- What the model "knows" from training only updates with new model releases, so changes there take months.
- Rerun your prompt set every month. Track share of voice and how you're described, not one-off answers, because responses vary from run to run.

**Where to start this week:** run the prompt audit, list the 10–20 most-cited third-party sources, and start working through them. That's usually where the competitor's lead comes from.

prompt: Does structured data or schema markup help a site get cited in Google AI Overviews and ChatGPT search?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
# Short answer: it helps a little, indirectly. It isn't a citation lever.

## What the platforms say

- **Google AI Overviews / AI Mode:** Google's guidance is that you don't need special markup to appear in AI features. The normal Search requirements apply: the page must be indexed, eligible to show a snippet, and helpful. Google does say structured data helps it understand pages, and recommends that markup match the visible content. It does not name schema as a ranking or citation factor for AI Overviews.
- **ChatGPT search:** It relies heavily on a search index (largely Bing) plus its own crawler (OAI-SearchBot). When it pulls a page, the model mostly reads the rendered text. There's no public evidence that JSON-LD by itself raises your chance of being cited.
- **Industry studies** show correlations between schema and AI citations. But sites that bother with schema also tend to do everything else well, so cause and effect aren't established.

## Where schema does earn its keep

1. **Entity clarity.** `Organization`, `Product`, `Person`, and `sameAs` links help search engines connect your brand, products, and authors. That feeds the knowledge graphs AI answers draw from.
2. **Factual attributes.** Price, availability, ratings, specs, and dates in `Product`/`Offer` markup make you easier to use in shopping and comparison answers, especially in Google and Bing.
3. **Rich results in classic search.** These still drive clicks, and the underlying rankings influence which pages AI systems retrieve.
4. **Low cost.** It's cheap to implement and rarely hurts, as long as it's accurate.

## What moves AI citations more

- Being indexed and crawlable. Don't block Googlebot, Bingbot, or OAI-SearchBot, and don't hide key content behind JavaScript or logins.
- Clear, quotable answers near the top of the page: definitions, comparisons, specs, pricing, FAQs written as plain text.
- Original data, benchmarks, and expert-authored content that others reference.
- Third-party mentions in reviews, comparison articles, Reddit, YouTube, and analyst coverage. AI answers lean hard on these.
- Fresh content with visible update dates.

## Practical setup

- **Implement:** Yoast or Rank Math (WordPress), or Schema App (enterprise, multi-site). Prioritize `Organization`, `Product`/`SoftwareApplication`, `Article` with author, and `BreadcrumbList`. FAQ markup no longer gets rich results for most sites, but the visible Q&A content is still useful.
- **Validate:** Google's Rich Results Test and Schema.org's Schema Markup Validator.
- **Measure AI visibility:** Profound, Peec AI, or Otterly.ai for tracking citations across ChatGPT, Perplexity, and AI Overviews. Semrush's AI Toolkit or Ahrefs Brand Radar are good options if you already pay for those suites.
- **Check indexing:** Google Search Console and Bing Webmaster Tools. Bing matters because of ChatGPT.

## Bottom line

Do schema as hygiene, but don't sell it internally as the AI-visibility strategy. Spend most of the effort on crawlability, answer-first content, original data, and earning third-party mentions. Then track citations directly so you can see what actually moves.

prompt: How do we change what an AI model says about us from its training data, not just what it finds when it searches the web?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**You can influence what future models learn about your company, but you generally can’t directly change what an existing third-party model learned during training.** There’s no equivalent of submitting an updated webpage and having its internal knowledge refresh.

The practical approach depends on whose model you want to change:

| Your target | What you can do | Main limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Public models such as ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini | Improve the public information available for future training; report specific factual errors to the provider | You don’t control what gets included or when a new model is trained |
| An AI assistant your company operates | Supply authoritative context through instructions or a knowledge base; fine-tune where appropriate | Changes affect your assistant, not everyone else’s |
| A model you train or control | Update training data and retrain, or investigate model-editing methods | Requires technical work and testing for unintended effects |

For a marketing team, I’d do five things:

1. **Establish what models actually say without search.** Test your company name, category, competitors, and common buying questions. Record the model, date, prompt, whether search was enabled, and the answer. Repeat tests—one answer isn’t a reliable baseline.

2. **Separate factual errors from positioning gaps.** “They discontinued this product” needs correction. “They aren’t mentioned among leading vendors” is a broader awareness and reputation problem. Different remedies apply.

3. **Publish a consistent, substantive factual record.** Maintain clear product descriptions, documentation, company facts, dated announcements, and evidence-backed customer stories. Make old or conflicting information clearly historical. This creates better material for potential future training, without guaranteeing inclusion.

4. **Build independent corroboration.** Accurate reporting, industry references, substantive reviews, and relevant public research can reinforce your company’s identity and claims. Prioritize credible evidence over flooding the web with repetitive promotional content.

5. **Submit documented errors to providers.** Include the exact prompt, incorrect answer, and authoritative evidence. This gives providers an actionable correction report; it does **not** guarantee a change to model weights.

For measurement, **Google Sheets** is enough to maintain an initial prompt-and-answer benchmark. **Promptfoo** is useful when you want repeatable tests across models and releases, so you can distinguish a lasting improvement from answer variability.

One important caution: **fine-tuning is usually better for teaching an assistant behavior, tone, and response patterns than maintaining changing company facts.** For your own assistant, an authoritative knowledge base is generally easier to update and audit.

Treat this as a long-term accuracy and reputation program. Be skeptical of agencies promising guaranteed placement in a model’s training data or a rapid “retraining” of public AI models.

prompt: Is llms.txt worth adding to our site for AI visibility?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Short answer:** It's cheap to add, so add it if it takes less than an hour. Just don't expect it to improve your visibility in AI search. The evidence so far shows almost no measurable benefit.

## What the evidence says (as of Oct 2026)
- **AI crawlers rarely request the file.** Ahrefs tracked about 137K domains and found that 97% of llms.txt files got zero requests from AI crawlers in a month. Another analysis of more than 500M AI bot events found only about 408 requests for llms.txt. GPTBot, ClaudeBot and PerplexityBot mostly just fetch your normal HTML pages. ([RichDevTools](https://richdevtools.com/articles/web/llms-txt-evidence-2026), [Something Inc](https://somethinginc.com/blog/llms-txt-97-percent-never-read/))
- **No link to being cited.** SE Ranking looked at about 300K domains. About 10% had the file, and having it made no clear difference to whether a site got cited in AI answers. ([Stan Ventures](https://www.stanventures.com/news/new-study-finds-llms-txt-has-no-clear-impact-on-ai-citations-5882/), [1ClickReport](https://www.1clickreport.com/blog/llms-txt-evidence-2026))
- **Google doesn't use it.** Gary Illyes said Google doesn't support it and has no plans to. John Mueller compared it to the keywords meta tag. OpenAI and Anthropic haven't publicly committed to reading it either. One vendor (Profound) says it has seen OpenAI and Microsoft fetch it, but treat that as a weak signal.
- **Where it does get used:** Ahrefs' logs suggest the main readers are AI coding tools and agents, like Cursor and Claude Code, looking up documentation.

## My recommendation
- **If you have developer docs or an API:** yes, add llms.txt and llms-full.txt to your docs site. Coding agents do use them. Mintlify and GitBook generate them automatically.
- **If it's a marketing site:** it's optional. On WordPress, Yoast and Rank Math can generate one in a few clicks, so the cost is close to zero. Just don't count it as an AI-visibility win in your reporting.

## What actually affects AI visibility
1. **Make sure AI crawlers can get in.** Check robots.txt and your CDN or WAF. Cloudflare now blocks AI bots by default, which has quietly hidden a lot of sites.
2. **Serve real HTML.** Many AI crawlers don't run JavaScript, so content that only renders client-side can be invisible to them.
3. **Be indexed in Bing and Google.** ChatGPT and Copilot search lean on Bing. Submit your sitemap to Bing Webmaster Tools and use IndexNow.
4. **Write pages that are easy to quote.** Clear comparison pages, pricing, FAQs, and specific facts stated directly.
5. **Get mentioned elsewhere.** Reviews (G2), Reddit, analyst and press coverage, and "best X" listicles. These drive citations far more than anything on your own site.
6. **Measure it.** Profound, Peec AI, Otterly, or Semrush's AI toolkit will show whether ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI Overviews actually mention you.

Many of the sources above are SEO and GEO vendors, but the main findings (Ahrefs, SE Ranking, Google's own statements) all point the same way.

Sources:

- [Something Inc: 97% never read](https://somethinginc.com/blog/llms-txt-97-percent-never-read/)

- [Pixis: What the evidence actually shows](https://pixis.ai/blog/does-llms-txt-help-ai-citations-what-the-evidence-actually-shows/)

prompt: What kind of content makes AI assistants more likely to recommend a product?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
AI assistants recommend products that are easy to retrieve, easy to quote, and backed up by sources other than the vendor. The second part matters more than most people expect: what others say about you usually counts for more than what your own site says.

## 1. Your own content: write passages an AI can lift and quote

- **One clear claim per passage, with the product named.** AI engines tend to pull single passages, not whole pages ([Elevarus](https://elevarus.com/generative-engine-optimization-citation-signals-vs-seo/)). Write "Acme supports SSO via SAML and OIDC on all plans," not "It also handles that, as mentioned above."
- **Specific numbers, sources and quotes.** The original academic GEO paper (Princeton et al., 2023) found that adding statistics, citations and quotations raised visibility in AI answers by up to about 40%. Keyword stuffing didn't help. Agency write-ups from 2026 say the same thing: cited content is "source-rich, specific, with clear entity signals" ([Dupple](https://www.dupple.com/learn/ai-search-visibility-chatgpt-perplexity)).
- **Pages that match how people actually prompt.** Buyers ask things like "best X for Y," "X vs Y," "does X integrate with Z," or "X pricing." That makes these the highest-value pages:
  - Comparison pages that are honest about where competitors are stronger
  - "Best for [use case / industry / team size]" pages
  - Public pricing, plan limits and feature tables. If pricing is hidden, the AI guesses or leaves you out.
  - Integration and compatibility pages
  - FAQs written in plain question-and-answer form
- **Keep it fresh.** An Ahrefs study of about 17M cited URLs found that AI assistants cite noticeably newer pages than Google's organic results do ([Crowdo summary](https://crowdo.net/blog/?p=2755)). Date your pages and actually update them.
- **Make it easy to crawl.** Use server-rendered HTML, keep key facts out of PDFs, images and gated pages, and don't block AI crawlers like GPTBot or PerplexityBot unless you mean to.

## 2. Third-party content: usually the bigger lever

When someone asks "what's the best X," the AI largely reflects the wider web's consensus. Priorities:
- **Review sites** like G2, Capterra and TrustRadius, plus category-specific ones. You want volume and recent reviews.
- **"Best X tools" listicles** and analyst or industry roundups. Being listed is often what decides whether you get recommended.
- **Reddit, forums and community Q&A.** Answers draw heavily on these. Show up genuinely and don't astroturf.
- **Consistent positioning everywhere.** Describe your category and your ideal customer the same way on your site, in reviews, in press and on Wikipedia/Wikidata if you qualify. Mixed signals weaken the AI's sense of what you are.
- **Original research or data that others cite.** This earns mentions and makes you the source behind a claim.

## 3. Measure before and after

Visibility varies by engine. Doing well in Google AI Overviews doesn't mean ChatGPT will cite you ([Substack analysis](https://ladyintechverse.substack.com/p/generative-engine-optimisation-how)). So track prompts in each engine separately:
- **[Profound](https://nogood.io/blog/best-tools-for-llm-visibility/):** the best-funded tool in the category and aimed at enterprises. It covers 9+ engines, though the reported $99 entry tier covers ChatGPT only.
- **Peec AI:** tracks visibility, position and sentiment, is strong for multiple countries, starts around €89–95/month, and lets you choose which engines to pay for ([Meltwater](https://meltwater.com/en/blog/llm-tracking-tools)).
- **Otterly.ai:** the cheapest way to start, at about $29/month ([Rivo](https://www.rivo.io/blog/ai-visibility-tracking-tools)).
- **Ahrefs Brand Radar:** a sensible choice if you already pay for Ahrefs.

Prices change often, so check the vendor sites.

## A caveat

Most "GEO" advice comes from agencies and tool vendors, and the evidence is still thin ([Crowdo](https://crowdo.net/blog/?p=2755)). Treat specific numbers as rough guides. Run your own test: pick about 30 buyer prompts, record a baseline, change a set of pages and third-party placements, and re-measure after 6–8 weeks.

**Where to start:** honest comparison and use-case pages, public pricing, and a push for reviews and listicle placements in your category.

prompt: How should we prioritize fixes to improve how AI assistants describe our product?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
Prioritize **errors that change a buyer’s decision**, then improve coverage and positioning. A wrong claim about pricing or capabilities usually deserves attention before a missing brand mention.

Start with 20–30 questions drawn from sales calls: “What does this product do?”, “Who is it for?”, “Does it integrate with X?”, and “How does it compare with Y?” Test them in the assistants your buyers use, repeating each a few times. Save the answer, date, whether web search was used, and cited sources.

Use this fix order:

| Priority | What to fix | Practical action |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Material inaccuracies** | Wrong pricing, capabilities, availability, security claims, or product identity | Correct the relevant public page. Make the answer explicit, including limitations and an updated date. |
| **2. Sources assistants cannot access** | Important facts hidden behind login, blocked crawlers, or inaccessible pages | Have web engineering check crawling, indexing, and readable page content. OpenAI specifically identifies allowing **OAI-SearchBot** as a requirement for inclusion in ChatGPT summaries and snippets. [Publisher guidance](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/12627856-publishers-and-developers-faq) |
| **3. Conflicting or stale information** | Different claims across your homepage, docs, pricing, listings, and reviews | Establish one authoritative page for each key fact; update conflicting pages and request corrections from external publishers. |
| **4. Missing buying context** | Correct descriptions that omit your audience, strongest use cases, differentiators, or limitations | Add concise, evidence-backed explanations, integration documentation, and fair comparison pages that answer actual buyer questions. |
| **5. Wording and visibility refinements** | Generic phrasing, missing secondary benefits, or inconsistent mentions | Improve these after the consequential errors and information gaps are addressed. |

Within each priority, rank fixes by **buyer impact × frequency × confidence in the cause ÷ effort**. Treat that as a planning heuristic. An incorrect security certification should jump the queue even if observed only once.

Trace the source before assigning work. If an assistant cites an outdated pricing page, you have a concrete fix. If no source is visible, test the same question with web search enabled before assuming your website caused the answer. Track searched and unsearched answers separately.

For tools, start with **Google Search Console** to inspect Google indexing, **Bing Webmaster Tools’ AI Performance report** to see cited pages and grounding queries across supported Microsoft experiences, and a spreadsheet to score answer accuracy. Bing’s report measures citation activity; you still need to read the answers to assess correctness. [Bing documentation](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/ai-performance-9f8e7d6c)

Measure success primarily as **fewer material errors and more complete answers on important buyer questions**. Use citations, mentions, referral traffic, and conversions as supporting measures. Recheck the same prompt set weekly and after significant product changes.

Avoid making special “AI markup” your first project. Google says no special schema is required for its generative AI search features; clear, accessible, useful content remains the foundation. [Google guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide)

prompt: AI assistants mention our product but add caveats that steer buyers away. How do we address the objections they raise?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
AI assistants usually repeat what's said about you across the web: reviews, Reddit threads, comparison articles, docs, analyst write-ups. Caveats generally come from one of three sources: **outdated information**, **real weaknesses**, or **a gap where your side of the story isn't published**. Each needs a different fix.

## 1. Catalog the caveats systematically

Don't rely on a few screenshots. Run the prompts your buyers actually use ("best X for Y," "[you] vs [competitor]," "is [you] good for enterprise?", "[you] pricing," "[you] alternatives") across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot, and Google AI Overviews. Repeat them, since answers vary between runs.

Tools that automate this:
- **Profound**: strong on enterprise share-of-voice and citation tracking across many engines.
- **Peec AI** and **Otterly.ai**: lighter and cheaper, good for prompt tracking and sentiment.
- **Scrunch AI**: good at surfacing *why* you're described a certain way and which sources drive it.
- **Ahrefs Brand Radar** or **Semrush's AI toolkit**: useful if you already pay for either.

Tag each caveat by theme (pricing, scalability, support, missing feature, security, learning curve), frequency, and the prompts it appears in.

## 2. Trace each caveat to its source

Perplexity, ChatGPT search, Gemini, and AI Overviews cite sources, so check them. Common culprits:
- G2, Capterra, and TrustRadius reviews (often old ones)
- Reddit and Hacker News threads
- Competitor "X vs. Y" pages and affiliate listicles
- Your own outdated docs, pricing pages, or changelogs
- Old analyst reports

## 3. Apply the right fix

**If the caveat is outdated** (e.g., "lacks SSO" when you shipped it last year):
- Update your own pages first. Put clear, specific statements on feature, pricing, and security pages ("SSO via SAML and OIDC on all plans since March 2025").
- Publish dated changelogs and release notes.
- Ask the authors of high-ranking third-party comparisons for corrections. Many will update.
- Run a review campaign so recent G2 and Capterra reviews outweigh old complaints.
- Expect a lag. Search-grounded answers update within weeks, but answers from model training data can take months.

**If the caveat is true** (e.g., "expensive for small teams"):
- Don't try to bury it. You can't, and buyers who find out later churn.
- Address the tradeoff directly with your own framing: "Built for teams of 50+. Here's why smaller teams often choose [cheaper option] and when they switch to us." Honest positioning content tends to get cited because it answers the real question.
- Send the pattern to product. A caveat repeated across every AI assistant is market research you didn't pay for.

**If the caveat fills a gap** (no authoritative content from you exists):
- Write the pages AI assistants want to cite: honest comparison pages, "Is [product] right for [use case]?" pages, migration guides, a security and compliance hub, and transparent pricing.
- Use clear headings, direct answers near the top, specific numbers, and FAQ sections. Extractable, factual content gets cited more often.
- Earn independent coverage through analyst briefings, customer case studies on third-party sites, podcasts, and authentic community participation (not astroturfing Reddit, which backfires and gets you banned).

## 4. Prioritize by revenue impact

Fix caveats that appear in high-intent prompts first ("[you] vs. [main competitor]," "[you] for enterprise"). A caveat in a generic "what is X" answer matters less than one in a shortlist comparison.

## 5. Measure monthly

Track caveat frequency, sentiment, share of voice against competitors, and which sources get cited. Tie this to pipeline where you can, for example by adding "How did you hear about us?" options for AI assistants.

## What to avoid

- Spinning up fake reviews or seeded forum posts. Platforms and models are increasingly good at discounting these, and the reputational risk is real.
- Hidden "instructions to AI" text on pages. It's ineffective and can be treated as spam.
- Vendors promising guaranteed placement in AI answers. Nobody can guarantee that.

**Quick start this week:** pull your top 20 buyer prompts, run them across 4–5 assistants, list the five most frequent caveats with their cited sources, and sort each into outdated, true, or gap. That list becomes your roadmap.

If you share the specific caveats you're seeing, I can help draft responses or content for each.

prompt: What does an answer engine optimization content strategy look like for a B2B SaaS company?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
An answer engine optimization (AEO) strategy for B2B SaaS should make your company **easy to discover, accurately describe, and credibly recommend when buyers ask AI tools for help.** The goal is qualified consideration and pipeline—not simply more citations.

Treat it as an extension of SEO and product marketing. Google explicitly says its AI search features require no special optimization or dedicated schema beyond established SEO practices. [Google’s guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

Here’s the strategy I’d recommend.

**1. Build your content plan around buying questions.**

Start with sales calls, customer interviews, support tickets, and lost-deal feedback. Identify 30–50 questions your ideal customers ask, including the context that changes the answer: company size, industry, existing stack, budget, and security requirements.

For a workflow automation SaaS company:

| Buyer need | Example question | Content to create |
|---|---|---|
| Understand the problem | “How can finance reduce manual invoice routing?” | Practical guide with a worked example |
| Identify options | “Best invoice automation tools for a midmarket team using NetSuite?” | Use-case page with clear selection criteria |
| Compare vendors | “Vendor A vs. Vendor B for approval workflows?” | Factual comparison with tradeoffs |
| Validate fit | “Does this support SSO and regional data hosting?” | Public security and technical documentation |
| Justify purchase | “What’s the total cost and implementation effort?” | Pricing explanation, implementation guide, ROI case study |

Prioritize questions where you have strong product fit, meaningful differentiation, and evidence. Generic category definitions should take a smaller share of the plan.

**2. Give each important question a useful, evidence-backed answer.**

Update existing pages before producing dozens of new articles. A strong page typically includes:

- A direct answer near the top.
- Specific conditions: who the advice or product suits, and its limitations.
- Supporting evidence: screenshots, customer outcomes, original data, or technical documentation.
- Descriptive headings, comparison tables, and clear definitions where useful.
- An appropriate next step, such as a template, trial, or demo.

For example, replace “Our platform streamlines operations” with an explanation of the workflow, supported integrations, setup requirements, and a documented customer result.

These practices improve clarity and usefulness; they do not guarantee AI inclusion.

**3. Invest in information competitors cannot easily reproduce.**

Make original evidence a recurring part of the editorial calendar:

- Aggregated product benchmarks, with methodology and sample sizes.
- Customer case studies with baseline, timeframe, and measured outcomes.
- Practitioner guidance from implementation and customer success teams.
- Detailed integration, migration, and deployment documentation.
- Honest comparisons explaining when another approach might fit better.

Publish the core findings openly. You can gate a worksheet or consultation while keeping the information buyers need accessible.

**4. Keep product facts accessible and consistent.**

Maintain clear public pages for capabilities, pricing structure, integrations, security, implementation, and limitations. Assign owners to review changing claims.

Have your web team check indexing, internal links, readable text, and crawler access through your hosting and security systems. Google says pages must be indexed and eligible for search snippets to appear as supporting links in its AI features; it does not require special AI text files. [Technical requirements](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)

**5. Build credible coverage beyond your own website.**

Look at which sources appear in answers to your target questions. Pursue relevant opportunities: integration partner directories, industry publications, practitioner communities, and genuine customer reviews.

Contribute useful expertise and accurate product information. Avoid treating this as a campaign to manufacture mentions. Independent sources should corroborate your positioning and claims.

**6. Measure visibility, accuracy, and commercial outcomes separately.**

Use a small, repeatable measurement system:

| Layer | What to track |
|---|---|
| Visibility | Brand mentions, recommendations, and cited URLs across a fixed set of buyer questions |
| Accuracy | Whether answers correctly describe capabilities, audience, pricing, and limitations |
| Engagement | Identifiable AI referrals and their trial/demo conversion rates |
| Revenue | Qualified opportunities and customer-reported AI influence |

Run the same question set regularly across the answer engines your buyers use. Record date, market, and whether web search was enabled; repeat samples because answers vary. Treat this as a directional panel, not a census of buyer behavior.

Start with these tools:

- **Google Search Console:** diagnose indexing and monitor search performance. Google includes AI-feature traffic in its overall Web reporting, so this does not provide a clean standalone AEO attribution view. [Reporting guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features)
- **Bing Webmaster Tools:** inspect first-party citation activity and grounding queries across supported Microsoft AI experiences. Its AI Performance report measures citations, not ranking or commercial impact. [Report documentation](https://www.bing.com/webmasters/help/ai-performance-9f8e7d6c)
- **Google Analytics 4 plus your CRM:** connect identifiable referrals to conversions and opportunities. Add “Did an AI assistant influence your shortlist?” to discovery calls to capture influence that referral tracking misses.

**A practical first 90 days:** spend the first month establishing the question set, baseline, and technical fixes. In month two, improve 8–12 high-priority pages and publish one strong original evidence asset. In month three, distribute that evidence through relevant partners and publications, review visibility and pipeline signals, and expand the topics showing qualified interest.

Have product marketing own the buyer questions and positioning, content/SEO own publishing and discoverability, and subject-matter experts validate the evidence. That gives you a sustainable program tied to how customers actually buy.

prompt: How can I see the web search results an AI assistant gets for a question before it writes its answer, to understand why we're missing?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
You can see this most reliably in an assistant’s **search or tool trace**: the queries it ran, the results returned, and the pages it opened before drafting its answer. The citations in the final answer show only part of that process.

For a marketing visibility audit, use two approaches:

- **Inspect the assistant’s search activity.** Expand any search activity or sources panel it provides. This can reveal queries and pages consulted, though consumer assistants don’t always expose every result or the complete text they received. Asking “show your searches and sources” can help, but it isn’t a guaranteed raw log.
- **Run a controlled search workflow.** Have a developer log the search response before passing it to the model. **Tavily** offers search results and extracted content suited to AI workflows; **Exa** is useful for semantic searches that find relevant pages beyond exact keyword matches; **SerpAPI** is useful for inspecting conventional search engine results. These help diagnose discoverability, but they won’t exactly reproduce another assistant’s private search pipeline.

For each question, capture this sequence:

**User question → actual search queries → returned URLs and snippets → pages read → final mentions and citations**

That lets you identify where you’re missing:

| What you observe | What to investigate |
|---|---|
| Your pages never appear | Indexing, relevance to the assistant’s queries, and presence on third-party sites |
| Your page appears but isn’t read | Whether its title and snippet clearly address the question |
| Your page is read but you aren’t mentioned | Whether the content gives clear, specific evidence that supports recommending you |
| Competitors are mentioned through third-party pages | Which comparison sites, reviews, or publications influence the answer |

**Start with 10–20 real buyer questions and repeat each a few times.** Record the assistant, model, date, and search settings. Results vary, so a recurring pattern is more useful than one missing mention.

The key limitation: a search API can show exactly what *your test workflow* received. Only the assistant provider’s own exposed trace can show what that particular assistant actually received.

prompt: Which third-party sites matter most for getting cited by AI search engines?

brand.name: Cheap Seats
brand.about: Cheap Seats is an open-source, self-hosted tool that asks AI assistants a brand's buyer questions, grades whether they recommend the brand, and builds a ranked list of fixes.

answer:
**Reddit, YouTube, Wikipedia, and the review sites and publishers in your category matter most—but your buyers’ questions should determine the priority.** A site that dominates general AI citations may have little influence on recommendations for your product.

Recent data supports that distinction: Ahrefs’ September 2026 ChatGPT study puts Reddit and Wikipedia first and second, while its cross-platform tracking shows a different mix by engine. Treat rankings as a starting point, not a universal outreach list. ([ChatGPT study](https://ahrefs.com/blog/most-cited-domains-in-chatgpt/), [cross-platform tracker](https://ahrefs.com/benchmarks/ugc-citations))

For a product marketing team, I’d prioritize these:

| Third-party sites | When they matter most | Practical action |
|---|---|---|
| **Category publications and comparison sites**—for example, PCMag, TechRadar, or specialist trade publications | “Best product for…,” comparisons, and buying advice | Identify the specific articles AI answers already cite. Earn inclusion through product testing, differentiated evidence, and useful reviewer briefings. |
| **G2, Capterra, TrustRadius** | B2B software evaluation and alternatives searches | Keep profiles accurate and encourage detailed, authentic customer reviews describing use cases, strengths, and limitations. |
| **Reddit and specialist forums** | Real-world experience, troubleshooting, and “is it worth it?” questions | Participate transparently in relevant communities. Answer specific questions and support customers; avoid manufactured recommendations. |
| **YouTube** | Demonstrations, tutorials, and product comparisons | Work with credible reviewers and publish clear demonstrations with descriptive titles, captions, and transcripts. Independent coverage adds a separate perspective. |
| **Wikipedia** | Company, product, and category background | Treat it as a reference source. Pursue independent coverage that establishes notability; suggest factual corrections transparently where appropriate. |

These are candidate channels, not a proven ranking for your business. Profound’s current research similarly recommends finding the particular niche publications, subreddits, and review pages cited in your category. ([Profound research guidance](https://www.tryprofound.com/articles/ai-marketing-agents-for-research))

**My recommended first step:** run 30–50 real buyer questions across ChatGPT search, Google AI Overviews/AI Mode, and Perplexity. Repeat them over several weeks and record the cited URLs, whether your brand appears, and how it is described. Prioritize sites that repeatedly appear on commercially relevant questions where competitors are included and you are absent.

You can start with a spreadsheet. For ongoing monitoring, **Ahrefs Brand Radar** is useful for discovering cited domains and pages; **Profound** is useful for tracking citations alongside brand mentions and answer accuracy. ([Ahrefs documentation](https://ahrefs.com/academy/how-to-use-brand-radar/cited-domains), [Profound documentation](https://help.tryprofound.com/articles/3443229936-answer-engine-insights-overview))

Measure **favorable, accurate inclusion in buyer answers**, not citation volume alone. An AI engine citing a publisher does not automatically mean it recommends every product that publisher covers.
